prompt.context: Our client, Shermer Pharma, is a venture-backed start-up pharmaceutical company. Over the past 15 years, Shermer has been developing a molecule that has been approved by the FDA to cure Alzheimer's with 90% efficacy. Shermer's owners have hired us to determine how they should sell their product and whether their product will be profitable.
prompt.question: How should Shermer Pharma sell its new Alzheimer's cure, and will the product be profitable?

clarifying_info.q: What exactly does the product do?
clarifying_info.a: It is a pill that cures Alzheimer's, an illness that currently has no treatment that cures or stops the progress of this disease. Alzheimer's is a degenerative, terminal disease that causes senility and dementia. 30 million people suffer worldwide.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the target customers / sales targets?
clarifying_info.a: Sales would be focused on neurologists and geriatric psychiatrists — not the consumer of the product.

clarifying_info.q: Does Shermer have an existing sales or marketing organization?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has purely been a research firm to this point. There is no Sales or Marketing organization.
Yes. FDA approval and related approvals have already been granted.
We will not focus on competitive response during this case. Shermer is the only firm with a cure for this illness and will be for the next 5 years.

exhibits.title: Sales Force Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two sales force options: Develop Own Sales Force vs. Contract Sales Force. Rows include: Percent of visit focused on our product, Fully loaded annual cost of 1 sales rep, Cost per sales call, Total calls required, Total Sales Reps needed, and Total annual Selling Cost. Some cells are blank and must be calculated.

exhibits.title: Annual Net Income
exhibits.shows: A five-year P&L table with rows for Projected Market Penetration, Total Users, Total Gross Margin, Amortized R&D Costs, Selling Costs, G&A Costs, and Net Income. Market penetration percentages are given for each year; all other rows are blank and must be calculated.

data.note: All other cells are blank. Additional data to be requested by the candidate and provided by the interviewer as earned.

framework: Split the problem into two parts: (1) Sales & Marketing strategy — how to sell the product; (2) Profitability — whether the product will generate sufficient profit
For Sales strategy, identify and compare the three options: build an internal sales force, contract an external sales force, or sell the company to a larger firm with existing commercial capabilities
For profitability, build a 5-year P&L: revenues (market size × penetration × gross margin per unit) minus amortized R&D, selling costs, and G&A
Key drivers to clarify: total addressable market size, market penetration trajectory, price/gross margin per unit, R&D investment, sales force cost structure, and G&A
Determine which sales approach yields the lowest cost and check whether cumulative profits by Year 5 cover the full R&D investment

questions.prompt: Market sizing (optional brain teaser): Estimate the size of the US Alzheimer's patient population that Shermer could sell to.
questions.guidance: Candidate should attempt a top-down estimate. Interviewer should allow the attempt and then provide the actual answer of 5 million patients (US addressable market) at the end of the exercise.

math.setup: Provide answer of 5MM after candidate attempts the sizing.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the missing cells to compare the total annual selling cost of building an internal sales force versus using a contract sales force.
questions.guidance: Candidate must fill in blank cells. For own sales force: derive cost per sales call from annual rep cost and calls-per-rep ratio, then multiply by total reps. For contract: double total calls (50% focus means 2x calls needed), then multiply by cost per call. Candidate should ask the interviewer for total calls required (100k) if not already given.

math.setup: Own sales force: each rep makes 100 calls/year at a fully loaded cost of $200k, so cost per call = $200k / (100 calls... but the exhibit shows 85 reps needed for 100k calls, so calls per rep = 100k/85 ≈ 1,176; cost per call = $200k*85 / 100k = $170). Contract: because reps only spend 50% of each visit on Shermer's product, total calls required doubles to 200k; at $60 per call total cost = $12MM.
steps: Own sales force cost per call: ($200k × 85 reps) / 100k calls = $170 per call
Own sales force total annual selling cost: $200k × 85 reps = $17MM
Contract: total calls required = 100k × 2 (50% focus) = 200k calls
math.answer: Own sales force: $17MM/year; Contract sales force: $12MM/year — contract saves $5MM/year

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 and the data provided, build the full 5-year P&L and determine in which year Shermer becomes profitable and whether R&D costs are recovered by Year 5.
questions.guidance: Candidate should request (or be given) the following inputs: Total Market = 5MM, Annual gross margin per user = $1,000, R&D Cost = $1.5B (amortized straight-line over 5 years = $300MM/year), Selling Costs = $12MM/year (contract sales), G&A = $25MM/year. Net Income = Gross Margin − R&D Amortization − Selling Costs − G&A. Candidate should note the loss in Year 1 and identify Year 2 as the first profitable year. Cumulative profit through Year 5 should be substantial, confirming full R&D recovery.

math.setup: Net Income = (Market × Penetration × $1,000 GM) − $300MM R&D amort − $12MM selling − $25MM G&A
math.answer: First profitable year is Year 2. Cumulative net income through Year 5 is ~$5.3B, well exceeding the $1.5B R&D investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What else should Shermer consider before engaging this plan? (High-level analysis at the end of the case.)

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: $1,000/year for a life-saving cure of a currently incurable ailment is likely underpriced — there may be significant room to raise price
Payer (insurance/Medicare) reimbursement rates and negotiation leverage should be assessed
Value-based pricing models could be explored given the curative outcome

categories.name: Sales force effectiveness
ideas: Contract sales organizations are typically less effective than internal sales forces
For an additional $5MM/year, Shermer could build its own sales force and potentially capture greater market share
The qualitative benefit of a dedicated sales force may outweigh the $5MM cost difference given revenues scaling to $3B

categories.name: Sell the company
ideas: Shermer's core competency is R&D, not commercialization
A larger pharma firm with an existing sales infrastructure could commercialize faster and at lower cost
Management's desire to retain ownership may override the financially optimal decision to sell

categories.name: Competitive & regulatory risks
ideas: 5-year exclusivity window before competitive response — need to maximize penetration quickly
Patent protection and lifecycle management strategy
Potential for label expansion to related neurological conditions

categories.name: Operational readiness
ideas: Manufacturing and packaging scale-up to meet projected demand (3MM users by Year 5)
Supply chain reliability for a novel molecule
Pharmacovigilance and post-approval safety monitoring requirements

recommendation: Shermer Pharma should pursue contract sales as the go-to-market approach, which costs $12MM/year versus $17MM for an internal force, reducing risk during the commercial launch phase

The product will be profitable: although Year 1 shows a net loss of $87MM, profitability begins in Year 2 and cumulative net income through Year 5 reaches ~$5.3B, fully recovering the $1.5B R&D investment
Alternatively (bonus answer), selling the company to a larger pharma firm with existing commercial infrastructure is the strategically optimal answer given Shermer's purely R&D-focused competency
risks: Contract sales reps split their time across multiple products (50% focus), which may limit penetration growth relative to projections
Year 1 net loss of $87MM requires adequate venture or debt financing to bridge
$1,000/year pricing may leave significant value on the table and could be revisited
next_steps: Negotiate contract sales organization terms and set performance milestones tied to penetration targets
Stress-test Year 1 cash needs and secure bridge financing
Explore pricing optimization — commission a payer landscape and willingness-to-pay analysis
Monitor competitive pipeline; reinforce patent protection and plan for lifecycle management after the 5-year exclusivity window
